implementation_notes: Rails ships the pattern as CurrentAttributes: a Current class declares the attributes it carries (account, user, request_id), the instance is isolated per thread or fiber through ActiveSupport::IsolatedExecutionState, and the framework resets it before and after each request so nothing leaks between them. Nested scoping is built in: Current.set(user: admin) { ... } exposes the override only inside the block and restores the previous values afterwards. The lower-level primitive is Fiber storage - Fiber[:key] / Fiber#[]= - which a newly created fiber inherits as a copy of the creating fiber's storage, so anything that hops execution state must be handed the values explicitly.
code_sketch:
class Current < ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes
  attribute :account, :user, :request_id
end

Current.user = authenticate(cookies)   # visible anywhere in the request
Current.set(user: admin) { audit! }    # block-scoped override, restored after
pitfalls: It is a global singleton for the execution state, so the documentation itself warns against stuffing controller-specific data into Current - keep it to a few top-level attributes or the model gets tangled.
Current.set must stay block-scoped; assigning the attributes directly leaves the override in place for the rest of the request.
Work handed to a raw Thread or a fresh Fiber starts from its own execution state and will not see (and cannot safely write) the request's values - pass them as job arguments instead.
